You are a professional biblical lexicographer fluent in Spanish. Translate the following English lexicon entry into Spanish.

Lemma: H6504

ENGLISH GLOSSES TO TRANSLATE:
  Terse gloss: "Divide, separate, scatter; to part ways, branch off, or cause division between persons or things"
  Readable gloss: "Built on the idea of splitting a unity into parts, this verb operates across multiple stems to express a wide range of separation. In the Nifal, Abram and Lot 'separated from each other' (Gen 13:9-14) and the nations 'were divided' after the flood (Gen 10:5, 32). The Hifil describes an agent who causes division — a whisperer who 'separates close friends' (Prov 16:28) or God who 'separated the nations' at creation (Deut 32:8). The Hitpael adds a reflexive dimension of scattering or coming apart, as when bones are 'disjointed' (Ps 22:14). Even a river 'divides into branches' (Gen 2:10), grounding the word in both geography and human relationship."

SENSES:
  Sense 1: "separate from one another"
    Enriched: Nifal reflexive/reciprocal: two parties part company or go separate ways. Gen 13:9-14 narrates Abram and Lot's parting; Gen 10:5, 32 describes post-flood nations dividing. Spanish 'sepárate' and 'es separado' mirror the mutual or self-directed separation. 2 Sam 1:23 poignantly notes that Saul and Jonathan 'were not divided' even in death, using the negative to underscore inseparable loyalty.
    Existing Spanish translations: Sepárate, el-que-se-separa, es-separado, fueron-separados, se-separaron, se-separarán, se-separó, separarse, y-se-separaron
  Sense 2: "cause to separate"
    Enriched: Hifil causative: an agent actively divides or separates others. Deut 32:8 recalls when the Most High 'separated the sons of Adam'; Prov 16:28 warns that a whisperer 'separates close friends.' Spanish 'separa' and 'cuando separó' capture the causative force. Ruth 1:17 invokes death as the only power that can 'part' Ruth from Naomi, elevating the verb to covenantal language.
    Existing Spanish translations: aparta, cuando-separó, separa, separará, separó, y-separaron
  Sense 3: "be scattered abroad"
    Enriched: Hitpael and Nifal participial: being scattered or dispersed as a group across space. Neh 4:19 describes workers 'scattered' along the wall; Ps 92:9 declares that evildoers 'will be scattered.' Spanish 'dispersos' and 'serán dispersados' emphasize the resultant state of wide dispersion rather than a single act of parting.
    Existing Spanish translations: dispersos, se-dispersan, serán-dispersados
  Sense 4: "spread out or dispersed"
    Enriched: Qal passive and Pual: a state of being spread apart physically. Ezek 1:11 describes the living creatures' wings as 'spread out' (perudoth) above; Esth 3:8 characterizes the Jews as 'dispersed' among the peoples. The spatial imagery distinguishes this from interpersonal separation, focusing on physical extension across an area.
    Existing Spanish translations: extendidas, y-separado
  Sense 5: "become disjointed"
    Enriched: Hitpael: coming apart or being dislocated, as when joints separate under duress. Ps 22:14 laments 'all my bones are disjointed' — a visceral image of suffering on the cross that the multilingual evidence renders as physical dislocation. Job 41:17 asks whether Leviathan's scales 'can be separated,' using the same stem to describe structural cohesion that resists pulling apart.
    Existing Spanish translations: se-separan, y-se-descoyuntaron
  Sense 6: "withdraw independently"
    Enriched: Piel: voluntarily withdrawing or going apart on one's own initiative. Hos 4:14 warns against the men who 'go apart' with prostitutes, emphasizing deliberate personal departure from the community for illicit purposes. Spanish 'se apartan' captures the reflexive voluntary quality. This singleton usage in the Piel gives the stem a moral coloring absent from the neutral Nifal separations.
    Existing Spanish translations: se-apartan
  Sense 7: "divide into branches"
    Enriched: Nifal of geographic branching: a single river dividing into multiple streams. Gen 2:10 records that a river 'went out of Eden' and there 'it divided' into four headwaters. Spanish 'se dividía' and German 'teilte er sich' reflect the physical splitting of a watercourse. This concrete, spatial sense may be the root metaphor from which the interpersonal and abstract senses developed.
    Existing Spanish translations: se-dividía
